rationale: All three require the entity to identify, document, and approve its cybersecurity strategy (with head-of-entity sponsorship) — the same atomic requirement.
Both require executing an action plan to operationalize/implement the approved cybersecurity strategy.
Both require reviewing the cybersecurity strategy at planned intervals or upon legislative/regulatory change.
All require establishing a dedicated cybersecurity department/function within the entity.
All require filling all cybersecurity positions with full-time, qualified (Saudi/nationally eligible) professionals.
Both require establishing a cybersecurity supervisory committee under the authorized official to ensure compliance, support, and monitoring.
Both require the authorized official to identify, document, and approve the cybersecurity governance structure, roles, and responsibilities.
All require reviewing and updating cybersecurity roles and responsibilities at planned intervals or upon legislative/regulatory change.

All three require an overall/overarching information security policy to be established, published, maintained, and disseminated to all relevant personnel to direct the organization's security posture.
Both require cybersecurity policies to be supported by technical security standards (e.g., firewall rule standards) to enable consistent/enforceable implementation.
Both require cybersecurity policies and procedures to be reviewed and updated at planned intervals or upon changes to legislative, regulatory, or standards requirements.
Both require the cybersecurity department to identify, document, and obtain approval of cybersecurity policies and procedures including controls and requirements.
All three require the cybersecurity department to identify, document, and approve the entity's risk management methodology and procedures, differing only in incidental phrasing of purpose.
Both mandate applying cybersecurity risk assessment procedures at least at the early stage of technology projects to identify and treat risks before implementation.
Both require the entity to identify and comply with cybersecurity requirements arising from nationally approved international agreements or commitments.
Both require the cybersecurity department to periodically review implementation of cybersecurity controls to confirm their continued effectiveness.
Both require cybersecurity control implementation to be reviewed and audited by parties independent of the cybersecurity department.
Both require audit and review results to be documented and presented to the cybersecurity supervisory committee and the Authorized Official for oversight.
Both establish the same process to detect and address unauthorized assets on the network at least weekly by removing, quarantining, or authorizing them.
Both require maintaining a comprehensive inventory of the same asset classes (endpoints, servers, software, cloud) each with an assigned owner and classification.
Both require establishing and maintaining a detailed inventory of all licensed software installed on enterprise assets, with identical intent and scope.
Both require information and technology assets to be classified, labeled, and handled per legislative and regulatory requirements, expressing the same asset-classification safeguard.

Both require associating security and privacy attributes with information exchanged between systems and system components to enforce handling/protection decisions, the same attribute-binding-on-exchange control.
Both are CIS Control 2.1 with the identical requirement to establish and maintain a detailed inventory of all licensed software on enterprise assets.
Both are NIST CSF GV.RR-02 with verbatim-identical definitions on establishing, communicating, understanding, and enforcing cybersecurity roles, responsibilities, and authorities.
All three state the same requirement that cryptography requirements must incorporate at least the provisions of the NCA National Cryptographic Standards.
All express the same control of applying encryption to sensitive data and securely managing the associated cryptographic keys across their lifecycle.
Both require identifying, documenting, and approving cybersecurity requirements for protecting and handling entity data in line with legislative/regulatory obligations.
Both require implementing data-protection requirements according to each item's assigned classification level to ensure proportionate safeguards.
Both state the same outcome that the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected for stored information.
Both require minimizing account data storage through defined retention and disposal policies, procedures, and processes that limit how long stored data is kept.
Both require establishing and maintaining an inventory of all enterprise accounts (user, administrator, service) for oversight.
Both define a preferably automated access-provisioning process for new hire, rights grant, or role change.
Both require the account registration process to include supervisor or sponsor authorization before access is granted.
Both require organizational lifecycle management of identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware.
Both require identities to be proofed and bound to credentials according to the risk context of the interaction.
Both require multi-factor authentication for all access into the cardholder data environment.
Both require MFA for all external/remote (including VPN) access into the enterprise network.
Both require using unique passwords for every enterprise asset and never reusing them to contain credential compromise.
Both require the OIDC relying-party client to mitigate ID token replay attacks.
Both enforce a limit on consecutive invalid logon attempts with lockout to deter brute-force/credential guessing.
Both require authenticating all user access to system components via at least one factor (password, token, smart card, or biometrics) before granting access.
All three express the same minimum single-factor username-and-password authentication requirement for identity and access management before granting entity system access.
Both are CIS Control 6.3 with identical wording requiring MFA for all external/remote (VPN) access.
Both are CIS Control 10.1 with identical text mandating anti-malware software on all enterprise assets.
Both are NIST CSF ID.AM-08 with identical text on managing systems, hardware, software, services, and data throughout their life cycles.
Both express NIST CSF PR.AA-05: defining, managing, enforcing, and reviewing access permissions/entitlements in policy incorporating least privilege and separation of duties.
Both require configuring data access control lists on need-to-know with least privilege, near-verbatim identical wording.
Both state the PCI-DSS deny-by-default access control system for system components and the CDE based on need-to-know.
Both define the same least-privilege access control policy with periodic reviews and prompt revocation on termination, near-identical text.
Both describe the same ATT&CK technique 'Credentials from Web Browsers' (legacy T1503 = current T1555.003) with identical opening definition.
Both describe adversaries disabling Windows event logging to limit detection/audit data, near-verbatim identical technique text.
Both have identical title and require multi-factor authentication for all administrative access to enterprise assets, differing only in trivial phrasing of the protected-against threat.
Both require all changes to network connections and network security control configurations to be formally approved and managed through a controlled change process.
Both restrict inbound traffic to the cardholder data environment to only what is necessary and block all other traffic.
Both define and implement configuration standards for network security controls (firewalls) to enforce consistent secure baselines.
All three require logically or physically isolating and segmenting network segments using firewalls and defense-in-depth to control cybersecurity risks.
Both protect the confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information across communication paths against interception and tampering.
Both require identifying, documenting, and formally approving cybersecurity requirements for protecting information systems and processing facilities.
Both require implementing the approved information-systems-protection cybersecurity requirements to operationalize the documented safeguards.
Both require identifying, documenting, and approving cybersecurity requirements for mobile/BYOD devices before they connect to the entity's network.
Both require protecting workstations and servers from viruses, suspicious programs, and malware using modern endpoint anti-malware/EDR technologies.
Both require deploying and maintaining anti-malware software on all enterprise assets to prevent, detect, and remediate malicious code across endpoints and servers (CIS 10.1).
Both require anti-malware deployment on all system components except those identified in periodic evaluations as not at risk for malware (PCI DSS 5.2.1).
Both require configuring automatic anti-malware signature updates on all enterprise assets on a daily-or-more-frequent basis (CIS 10.2).
All four state CIS Control 4.1: establish and maintain a secure configuration process for enterprise assets and software with periodic documentation review.
Both require configuring/managing system components securely per industry-accepted hardening standards to reduce attack surface.
Both require changing vendor default accounts, passwords, and SNMP community strings before a system is installed on the network.
Both enforce least functionality: enable only necessary services, protocols, daemons, and functions and remove/disable all unnecessary functionality.
Both set the security option to deny all outgoing NTLM authentication traffic to remote servers.
Identical CIS 3.1 wording establishing and maintaining a data management process; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Identical CIS 3.3 wording configuring data access control lists by need-to-know under least privilege; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Identical NIST CSF GV.OC-01 subcategory text; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Identical NIST CSF GV.SC-01 subcategory text; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Identical NIST CSF ID.AM-03 subcategory text; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Identical NIST CSF ID.AM-05 subcategory text; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Identical NIST CSF ID.RA-03 subcategory text; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Identical NIST CSF ID.RA-10 subcategory text; one is the enterprise-labeled duplicate.
Both require analyzing and filtering inbound email with advanced mechanisms to block phishing and spam — the same anti-phishing email filtering control.
Both restrict usage to only fully supported, enterprise-approved web browsers and email clients — the same client-software approval control.
Both require identifying, documenting, and formally approving cybersecurity requirements for protecting the email service — the same requirements-definition control.
All three state the same ECC 2-15-1 control: cybersecurity requirements for protecting the entity's external web applications must be identified, documented, and approved.
Both require software-development personnel to be trained in software security and secure coding techniques per industry best practices and organizational requirements — identical wording.
All express CIS 16.1: establish and maintain a secure software development process whose acceptance criteria include peer code review and threat modeling.
Both are NIST PR.PS-06: secure software development practices are integrated into and their performance monitored throughout the software development life cycle.
Both require setting the Secure attribute on cookies so they are transmitted only over encrypted HTTPS, the same atomic safeguard.
Both verify security controls that prevent browsers from rendering HTTP response content or functionality in an incorrect context, the same control.
Both require verifying that received system components are genuine and unaltered to detect counterfeit or tampered parts in the supply chain.
Both require that event logging and monitoring requirements be identified, documented, and formally approved.
Both require operational implementation of the defined event logging and monitoring management requirements across the entity.
Both require activating/enabling event logging specifically for the entity's critical information assets so security-relevant activity is captured.
Both establish and maintain an enterprise audit log management process defining logging requirements (CIS 8.1).
Both collect audit logs and ensure logging is enabled across all enterprise assets per the audit log management process (CIS 8.2).
Both require audit logs be enabled and active for all system components and cardholder data access (PCI DSS 10.2.1).
Both describe reviewing audit logs for anomalies via automated mechanisms to enable timely detection of security incidents, in near-identical wording.
Both describe the same technique of persistence via startup folder or Registry run key executing at logon (MITRE T1547.001).
Both mandate that only currently vendor-supported software/components remain in use and that unsupported/end-of-life products be updated or replaced.
Both require that project management and technology-asset change cybersecurity requirements include, at minimum, vulnerability assessment and remediation.
Both require that cybersecurity requirements for technical vulnerability management be identified, documented, and approved by the appropriate authority.
Both require internal vulnerability scans performed at least once every three months to detect weaknesses in internal systems.
Both require periodic vulnerability assessment and detection to identify security weaknesses across systems on a recurring basis.
Both require establishing and maintaining a documented risk-based remediation strategy/process reviewed at least monthly to prioritize fixing vulnerabilities.
Both require establishing and maintaining a documented vulnerability management process for enterprise assets with documentation reviewed/updated at least annually.
Both require establishing and maintaining a penetration testing program scaled to enterprise size/complexity to identify exploitable weaknesses.
Both define penetration testing scope to cover all externally provided internet-facing services and their components.
Both describe the same generic phishing technique of sending phishing messages to trick users into revealing credentials or executing content to gain initial access to victim systems.
Both require incident and threat management requirements to be identified, documented, and formally approved by the relevant authority.
Both require incident and threat management to define documented incident response plans and escalation procedures for structured handling of incidents.
Both designate a primary person plus at least one backup to own and manage the enterprise incident handling process.
Both determine an incident's impact and magnitude to prioritize response and allocate resources proportionate to impact.
Both develop and obtain management approval of a formal incident response plan to enable rapid, effective handling of cybersecurity incidents.
Both mandate that business continuity requirements, at a minimum, ensure the continuity of cybersecurity systems and procedures through disruptive events.
Both require backup and recovery management requirements to be identified, documented, and approved.
Both require periodic review of the implementation of backup and recovery management requirements.
All three require backup scope to cover, at minimum, critical technology and information assets.
Both establish/maintain a data recovery process addressing scope, prioritization, and security of backup data (CIS 11.1).
Both require automated backups of in-scope enterprise assets at least weekly or more frequently by data sensitivity (CIS 11.2).
Identical PR.AA-01 requirement to manage identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware.

Both describe communicating incident information/notifications to designated internal teams and external parties to enable coordinated response, awareness, and regulatory reporting obligations during a security event.
Both require the entity to periodically develop and approve a multi-channel cybersecurity awareness program.
Both require establishing and maintaining a security awareness program to continuously educate the workforce on secure behavior.
Both require providing specialized skills and training to personnel in roles directly tied to cybersecurity.
Both require providing incident response training to personnel with incident handling duties.

Both require personnel cybersecurity requirements to be identified, documented, and approved before, during, and upon end/termination of employment — the same define-requirements control with near-identical wording.
Both require the defined personnel cybersecurity requirements to be implemented across all stages of the employment lifecycle — the same implement-requirements control.
Both require establishing and maintaining an inventory of service providers; 0148 is more complete, adding classifications and a designated enterprise contact.
All three mandate the same organizational risk assessment prior to acquiring or outsourcing information security services to evaluate third-party exposure.
Both establish a formal cybersecurity supply chain risk management program covering strategy, policies, and processes across the supplier lifecycle.
Both employ testing and analysis of supply chain elements, processes, and actors to detect weaknesses and tampering; 0690 states the broader, standalone requirement.
Both require that physical-security requirements protecting assets against unauthorized physical access, loss, theft, and damage be identified, documented, and approved.
All three restrict physical access to critical/sensitive facility areas to authorized personnel only.
Both are the clean-desk safeguard requiring sensitive/confidential information (paper or electronic) to be secured in the workspace.
